articles.author: CiciSee
articles.description:
Lately, I’ve been curious about how much of the content online is actually AI-generated. Some posts feel human, some feel… a bit robotic. I decided to try MyDetector.ai to see how it works in real life. After spending some time with it, here’s my experience, along with what I think could make it even better.
The site opens cleanly and immediately feels easy to use. No signup, no clutter, just a space to paste text or upload an image. I tried a few blog paragraphs, social media posts, and even a meme generated by AI — the results appeared in seconds.

1. Fast and effortless
2. Everything in one place
3. Clean design

1. Explain results better
2. Keep a history of results
3. Show changes in humanizer clearly
4. Mobile and accessibility
5. Transparency about limits
Compared to NoteGPT AI Detector and AIHumanizer, MyDetector.ai feels lighter and faster. It’s great for quick checks, while NoteGPT offers more features for handling full files, batch processing, and workflow integration. AIHumanizer focuses mostly on text, and its control options are limited compared to MyDetector’s humanizer.
Use MyDetector.ai for quick checks on social posts, blog snippets, or emails.
For longer documents or multiple files, consider combining it with NoteGPT to get more detailed feedback and batch capabilities.
When using the humanizer, always read the revised text to ensure it keeps your original meaning and tone.
Using MyDetector.ai felt like having a small helper for your writing. It’s fast, simple, and approachable — ideal for quickly checking whether content might be AI-generated or needs a more natural touch. With some improvements, like clearer explanations, history tracking, and a better humanizer view, it could become a tool you rely on every day.
https://mydetector.ai
articles.title: MyDetector.ai Deep Dive — Honest Experience with AI Detection and Humanizer

I.


In the winter of 1994, in a small apartment in Hong Kong, a fourteen-year-old boy plugged a US Robotics Sportster 14,400 Fax Modem into his family's telephone line. He had read about something called a "bulletin board system" in a PC magazine. He didn't fully understand what it was. He dialed anyway.
The modem screamed. Static. Then text appeared on his screen. A welcome message. A list of names he didn't recognize, discussing topics he barely understood.
He was terrified. He was hooked.
Over the next two years, that boy spent hundreds of hours on BBSes. He made friends he never met in person. The person running each board—the "sysop"—was usually just some guy with a spare computer. But that guy was there. You could page him. He knew your name.
That boy was me. And I've spent three de…

For the last two days, I’ve been learning the basics of JavaScript, and it has been really fun and easy to understand. These topics may look simple, but they are the building blocks for everything we will write in the future. So I wanted to share what I learned in a clear and beginner-friendly way.
1. Variables in JavaScript
let
Used for values that can change later.




let age = 20;
age = 21;

const
Used when the value should not be changed.




const PI = 3.14;


var
The old way of declaring variables.
Not recommended now because it creates confusion with scope.
2. Data Types in JavaScript
Primitive Types
String → "Hello"

Number → 23, 45.6

Boolean → true or false

Null → empty value
Undefined → no value assigned
BigInt → very large numbers
Symbol → unique values
Non-Primitive Types
Object
Array
Function
3. Undefined vs Null
undefined
Means a variable exists but has no value yet.




let x;
console.log(x); // undefined


null
Means intentionally empty.
We set it manually when something should have no value.




let data = null;

articles.description:
The spectre haunting higher education today isn’t plagiarism. That’s a problem of ethics and detection, and we’ve largely figured that out. The new spectre is far more insidious, far more dangerous — it’s the spectre of perfect output and an empty mind.
Picture this. You’re in a university seminar, and a student can, in seconds, conjure a 2,000-word essay on the geopolitical intricacies of the Treaty of Westphalia. The prose is impeccable, the arguments razor-sharp, the structure flawless. But then, the uncomfortable question arises — “Can you explain the third paragraph without looking at your screen?” The answer is often silence.
We are living through a profound uncoupling of doing from understanding. For centuries, the very act of labour — writing, calculating, coding — was the crucible…
